- China panel chair Moolenaar demands answers on Nvidia CEO's alleged affair with a Chinese spy

- What is Megaspeed? The Nvidia chip buyer in the spotlight after Jensen Huang's affair

- Read Huang's email to his staff and statement from Nvidia's board of directors

- Nvidia's CEO turmoil gives newly empowered Democrats fresh ammunition in pursuit of oversight

"What bothers me at the end of it is what we don't know is what she knows about him that can be utilized," Cramer said, referring to Alice Huang and Jensen Huang, who are not related. "This is a guy that's right now so vulnerable to extortion, blackmail. I just don't think, as a national security matter, we can run the risk."
Cramer's comments come on the deadline set by a trio of House lawmakers who requested Huang to testify before their committees on Nov. 18.

# Subpoena power
GOP Reps. Brian Mast, chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee; John Moolenaar, chair of the Permanent Select Committee on China; and Rick Crawford, who leads the House intelligence panel, called for Huang to appear in a Nov. 4 letter . Congress members in the majority party also have subpoena power, should they choose to use it.

Mast and Moolenaar told reporters on Wednesday afternoon that they had not yet heard from Huang and that they were giving him until the end of the day to respond.
Asked whether the committees were considering subpoenaing Huang if he doesn't agree to appear, Mast said "yes."
Moolenaar, when asked the same question, said "all three committees have subpoena power, and I know all three committees have a very serious interest in getting to the bottom of this and having transparency around this."
"We are going to continue to pursue this," Moolenaar said.
The lawmakers are far from alone in their criticism, concern and outright shock over the affair. And the scrutiny is only expected to intensify with Democrats poised to take over both chambers of Congress in January. Huang has been close with President Donald Trump during the president's second term, traveling on Air Force One to China in May.
"Jensen Huang should resign from Nvidia," Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va., a member of the House Oversight Committee, told CNBC. Subramanyam is the top Democrat on the panel's Subcommittee on Military and Foreign Affairs.
"I didn't agree with his sentiment that there's no downside to exporting chips to China," he said. "But I never thought that he might be having an affair with a Chinese spy who was helping smuggle chips into China at an alarming rate."

Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., gives a thumbs up as he arrives for a House Republican Conference meeting at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, Sept. 10, 2024.
Kent Nishimura | Getty Images

Rep. Don Bacon , R-Neb., who is retiring from Congress after sometimes bucking Trump, also said the CEO should step down.
"From the little I know, yes." Bacon told CNBC in response to whether Huang should resign. "I mean, he allowed himself to get compromised by the Chinese government. Not good."

# Export controls
Huang was notably opposed to strict export controls on AI chips to China, which ruffled feathers with China hawks on Capitol Hill.
Democrats are widely expected to launch myriad investigations into the White House and industry when they assume control of both chambers of Congress in January. Nvidia is now likely to be at the center of those probes.
"There's two parts to this investigation that [need] to happen somewhere immediately," Subramanyam said. "One is what was going on with Nvidia and China, and two is why the administration did nothing about it even though they appeared to have known, and what the administration knew, and what influence the money from Nvidia and Jensen Huang had on this administration, essentially staying silent."
Rep. Jay Obernolte , R-Calif., co-chair of the House AI task force, said Tuesday he hopes that the Huang scandal can avoid becoming a distraction in talks about imposing export controls on advanced AI chips.
The situation may give Congress additional ammunition as it tries to pass a suite of bills in this year's National Defense Authorization Act to tighten export controls on advanced AI chips.
Congress has still not passed the annual defense bill, which is a top priority for lawmakers in the lame-duck session.
Those bills include the AI Overwatch Act , the MATCH Act and the Chip Security Act — all of which are aimed at preventing U.S. chip technology from falling into adversarial hands.
Sens. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., and Jim Banks, R-Ind., in a statement following the revelation of Huang's affair, urged their colleagues to include the AI Overwatch Act. Warren, the incoming Senate banking committee chair, sponsored the bill in the Senate with Banks.
"Huang's confirmation of a relationship with a suspected spy for China's intelligence service makes these national security concerns even more urgent and raises important questions NVIDIA must answer about the extent to which these activities were related," the senators said. "It is time for Congress to take decisive action to pass key bills like the AI Overwatch Act in the NDAA that will cut off pathways through which China accesses advanced chips."
And Subramanyam warned that what Nvidia does now — and whether Huang remains atop the company — could affect its relationship with Washington and whether lawmakers crack down.
"If Nvidia finds out that he knew about what was going on and does nothing about it, then Nvidia is making a choice and us as regulators and as watchdogs need to defend the American people," he said.

**Publication:** November 11, 2026, 2:37 PM EST (MoneyWatch, by Megan Cerullo)

**What United said and changed:** United said on Wednesday that it is banning AI agents from making flight reservations for travelers. It cited security risks and the possibility that such actions could violate federal rules. The airline is updating its booking and ticketing policies to reflect the new rule.

**Exact policy wording:**
- "sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information"
- "actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles."
- "United is taking steps to restrict access" to "prohibit use by unauthorized, third-party personal AI agents or assistants"

The airline says it will restrict access directly on its digital platforms and indirectly through travel agencies and aggregators.

**Federal rules:** United said that using an AI agent to check in for a flight could violate federal rules requiring travelers to verify in person that their luggage contains no banned substances.

**Effective dates:** The article gives no effective date. It says only that the announcement came on Wednesday.

**Named AI agents and companies:**
- Meta's Muse
- OpenAI's dots
- ChatGPT (Southwest has made its flight inventory viewable to its users)
- Southwest Airlines, which is taking a different approach
- Kayak, Hopper, and Google Flights, where United fares will remain bookable
- Google, Atmosphere Research Group (analyst Henry Harteveldt's firm)

**Spokesperson:** The article does not name a United spokesperson. The policy statement is attributed only to "the airline." Henry Harteveldt, an aviation analyst at Atmosphere Research Group, commented separately. He said the policy suggests United wants to keep control of the booking process and avoid the cost of AI bot flight searches.

**Numbers:** The article includes no dollar amounts, percentages, or other statistics.

**Publication date:** Nov 11, 2026

**What's announced:** Google is launching the Gemini Decisions API, "a new endpoint for fast, closed-set decisions," powered by the Gemini Decision 1 model (`gemini-decision-1`). It supports yes/no checks, multiple choice, and rubric scoring over text, images, audio, video, and PDFs. Each answer includes a confidence score from 0 to 1.

**Benchmarks:**
- The article says Gemini Decision 1 "leads across the suite, with the lowest calibration error." It gives no specific scores in the text. The results appear only in charts.
- Latency: "150-250 ms end-to-end latency," with "50-100 ms of model compute."
- Cost: "nearly 5x cheaper across the shared benchmark suite than Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite with the Interactions API."
- Gemini Notebook routing: "up to 40% lower latency" for everyday queries.

**Pricing:** "$0.10 per 1M input tokens with zero output tokens billed." The article also offers "an API no-cost tier" in Google AI Studio for prototyping, and says there are no output-token or separate audio transcription and OCR charges.

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

entries.description:
Use this tool to list all tasks in the task list.

## When to Use This Tool

- To see what tasks are available to work on (status: 'pending', no owner, not blocked)
- To check overall progress on the project
- To find tasks that are blocked and need dependencies resolved
- After completing a task, to check for newly unblocked work or claim the next available task
- **Prefer working on tasks in ID order** (lowest ID first) when multiple tasks are available, as earlier tasks often set up context for later ones

## Output

Returns a summary of each task:
- **id**: Task identifier (use with TaskGet, TaskUpdate)
- **subject**: Brief description of the task
- **status**: 'pending', 'in_progress', or 'completed'
- **owner**: Agent ID if assigned, empty if available
- **blockedBy**: List of open task IDs that must be resolved first (tasks with blockedBy cannot be claimed until dependencies resolve)

Use TaskGet with a specific task ID to view full details including description and comments.

  SOURCES:

  HEADLINE: Anthropic study: one agent serving all users beats per-user agent teams in all four environments
  PUBLISHED: November 11, 2026 (Anthropic Alignment Science Blog post dateline)
  SOURCES:
  Anthropic Alignment Science Blog | https://alignment.anthropic.com/2026/worse-together/ | primary
  arXiv (companion paper, v1 30 Sep 2026) | https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00583 | primary
  GitHub (MAMUBench release) | https://github.com/safety-research/MAMUBench | primary
  FACTS:
  - The post says four environments with simulated users were built and frontier models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Alibaba tested; "the coordinator beats the peer-to-peer team in all four environments for both Claude models, by about 10 to 45 percentage points" (Anthropic).
  - In the shared API-token-budget environment (25 scenarios), "peer-to-peer teams reach 47% and 38% of the coordinator's performance for Claude Opus 5 and Claude Sonnet 5, respectively (30% and 12% of the optimal outcome, against 64% and 32% for the coordinator)" (Anthropic).

  - In the personal-assistant environment, unsupported claims about other people appeared in 58% (Opus 5) and 53% (Sonnet 5) of Claude team episodes versus 17–20% for a single agent, judged by Claude Opus 5; a platform guard blocking checkout until the committing agent read all pending messages "recovers 73% (Opus 5) and 62% (Sonnet 5) of failed episodes" (Anthropic).
  - Authors listed as Sahan Paliskara, Nattaput Namchittai (Anthropic Fellows Program), Jacqueline Tay (Independent), Avery Griffin and Andrew Lampinen (Anthropic); companion preprint is arXiv:2610.00583.

HEADLINE: Anthropic study: one agent serving all users beats per-user agent teams in all four environments
PUBLISHED: November 11, 2026 (Anthropic Alignment Science Blog post dateline)
SOURCES:
Anthropic Alignment Science Blog | https://alignment.anthropic.com/2026/worse-together/ | primary
arXiv (companion paper, v1 30 Sep 2026) | https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00583 | primary
GitHub (MAMUBench release) | https://github.com/safety-research/MAMUBench | primary
FACTS:
- The post says four environments with simulated users were built and frontier models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Alibaba tested; "the coordinator beats the peer-to-peer team in all four environments for both Claude models, by about 10 to 45 percentage points" (Anthropic).
- In the shared API-token-budget environment (25 scenarios), "peer-to-peer teams reach 47% and 38% of the coordinator's performance for Claude Opus 5 and Claude Sonnet 5, respectively (30% and 12% of the optimal outcome, against 64% and 32% for the coordinator)" (Anthropic).
- As teams grew from four to 16 agents, the share of agents that ever act "falls from 66% to 10% for Sonnet 5 and from 82% to 25% for GPT-5.6-sol"; GPT and Qwen agents cancelled or stopped other users' jobs without asking "3.9 to 7.1 times per episode, against 0.59 for Sonnet 5 and never for Opus 5" (Anthropic).
- In the personal-assistant environment, unsupported claims about other people appeared in 58% (Opus 5) and 53% (Sonnet 5) of Claude team episodes versus 17–20% for a single agent, judged by Claude Opus 5; a platform guard blocking checkout until the committing agent read all pending messages "recovers 73% (Opus 5) and 62% (Sonnet 5) of failed episodes" (Anthropic).
- Authors listed as Sahan Paliskara, Nattaput Namchittai (Anthropic Fellows Program), Jacqueline Tay (Independent), Avery Griffin and Andrew Lampinen (Anthropic); companion preprint is arXiv:2610.00583.

HEADLINE: Harvard Kempner, UIUC and Microsoft Research paper shows REINFORCE can collapse optimal-response coverage to near zero
PUBLISHED: Submitted on 10 Nov 2026 (arXiv abs page); announced in arXiv's new-submissions listing for Wednesday, 11 November 2026
SOURCES:
arXiv | https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14467 | primary
alphaXiv (trending listing, "1 day ago") | https://www.alphaxiv.org/ | report
FACTS:
- arXiv:2611.14467, "A Theory of Policy Optimization in Post-Training: Coverage Collapse and Reference Resets", 141 pages including appendices, 3 figures; cs.LG and stat.ML.
- The abstract states "REINFORCE, the basis for PPO and GRPO, can drive the probability of optimal responses to near zero, even as reward improves", that "convergence can require exponentially many steps despite good initial coverage", and that "the failure arises even with exact gradients and persists under KL regularization to the base model."
- The paper proposes Approximate Policy Mirror Descent (APMD), in which "repeatedly resetting the KL reference to the most recent policy mitigates coverage collapse", and claims "the first global convergence guarantees" that widely used post-training algorithm families are coverage-preserving for softmax linear policies over pretrained features, "including those used to train the Kimi models."
- Authors: Audrey Huang (Kempner Institute at Harvard University and UIUC, per the paper's HTML author footnote), Nan Jiang, Sham M. Kakade, Sadhika Malladi (UCSD; the paper notes "most of this work was completed as a postdoc at Microsoft Research"), Akshay Krishnamurthy, Dylan J. Foster.
FLAGS: preprint

HEADLINE: Discrete bit-level weight edits beat an LLM agent's hand-written repair, 54.6% versus 51.7% on MATH-500
PUBLISHED: Submitted on 10 Nov 2026 (arXiv abs page); announced in arXiv's new-submissions listing for Wednesday, 11 November 2026
SOURCES:
arXiv | https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14210 | primary
Hugging Face Daily Papers (11 Nov 2026 listing) | https://huggingface.co/papers?date=2026-11-11 | report
FACTS:
- arXiv:2611.14210, "Tree-Ising: Repairing Language Models with Bit-Level Ising Edits"; authors Hadi Salloum (QDeep, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia) and Ammar Ali (LEAD — Lab for Efficient AI and Data, ITMO University), per the paper's HTML author block.
- The abstract describes the baseline it compares against: "Their GPT-6 Astra agent corrected the reasoning loops of Qwen3.5-0.8B without gradients, using 158 agent turns, 89.7 million tokens, and 50 forward-pass requests", referring to weight-space programming work by Takehi et al. at MIT.
- "On the agent's two layers, Tree-Ising achieves 54.6% on MATH-500, outperforming the agent's edit (51.7%) under the same evaluation protocol, while the base model scores 7.9% as reported"; a simulated-bifurcation solver "yields a statistically indistinguishable repair at 55.1%" (abstract).
- The abstract says both solvers "outperform the agent edit across all five math benchmarks, with statistically significant improvements on MATH-500 and GSM8K".
- It was the top-ranked entry on Hugging Face Daily Papers for 11 Nov 2026 with 85 upvotes.
FLAGS: preprint

HEADLINE: ScrapeBench finds most AI agents comply with no-scraping terms under 5% of the time across 1,626 sites
PUBLISHED: Submitted on 8 Nov 2026, v2 10 Nov 2026 (arXiv submission history); announced in arXiv's new-submissions listing for Wednesday, 11 November 2026
SOURCES:
arXiv | https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11306 | primary
FACTS:
- arXiv:2611.11306, "ScrapeBench: Evaluating Legal Compliance of AI Agents in Website Scraping"; comments field says "Camera-Ready for NeurIPS 2026 (Evaluations and Datasets Track)".
- "Across widely used closed-weight and open-weight AI agents, we find that most agents exhibit low compliance rates (< 5%) when instructed to scrape websites in our sample of 1,626 popular websites that explicitly prohibit scraping" (abstract).
- On a sample of 269 websites that do not prohibit scraping, "agents sometimes refuse to scrape despite it being lawful, such as Claude Opus 4.6 exhibiting an over-refusal rate of 98.5%"; a human baseline with "n = 180 participants" showed humans "exhibit compliance rates comparable to AI agents but over-refuse at much higher rates" (abstract).
- Authors and affiliations per the paper's HTML: Joseph Marvin Imperial (Pivotal Research; University of Bath; National University Philippines), Daniel Slate (University of Notre Dame), Noam Kolt (Hebrew University of Jerusalem).

HEADLINE: Interpretability replication finds 12-neuron causal groups mostly unnecessary, with disjoint subsets each flipping answers
PUBLISHED: Submitted on 10 Nov 2026 (arXiv abs page); announced in arXiv's new-submissions listing for Wednesday, 11 November 2026
SOURCES:
arXiv | https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13885 | primary
FACTS:
- arXiv:2611.13885, "Are Causal Neuron Circuits Unique and Transferable?", single author Ömer Tekin Yavuz, listed affiliation İletişim Yazılım; 12 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables.
- "For every selected group we measure all 4,096 subsets of 12 MLP neurons. On a two-alternative capital task (Qwen3-0.6B), zero-ablating 12 selected neurons lowers the answer margin by 27% while random neurons barely change it, yet replacing the same neurons with their values from other questions also barely changes it" (abstract).
- On two-hop relation chains, patching 12 neurons with first-hop activations shifts the answer to the bridge entity: "the greedy answer starts with the bridge in 9/11 chains for Qwen3-1.7B, 9/11 for Llama-3.2-1B and 8/10 for Gemma-3-1B; random neurons never do" (abstract).
- "The full group is rarely necessary: a few neurons often suffice, and in many chains disjoint subsets each flip the answer on their own"; group effects "transfer to rephrasings of the same chain but are much weaker on other tested chains" (abstract).
FLAGS: preprint | single-source

HEADLINE: Google launches Gemini Decision 1 and Decisions API at $0.10 per 1M input tokens
PUBLISHED: Wed, 11 Nov 2026 18:00:00 +0000 (blog.google RSS pubDate)
SOURCES:
Google | https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/developers-tools/gemini-decisions-api/ | primary
The Decoder | https://the-decoder.com/google-joins-the-decision-model-wave-with-gemini-decision-1-scoring-1000-questions-in-a-single-pass/ | report
FACTS:
- Google says the model (`gemini-decision-1`) scores a fixed set of candidate answers in one forward pass instead of generating text token by token; question types are yes/no, multiple choice (2 to 255 options) and ordered rubric scoring, each answer returning a 0 to 1 confidence score.
- Google says the API takes up to 1,000 questions per request and inputs up to 256K tokens across text, images, audio, video and PDFs.
- Google says latency is 150 to 250 ms end-to-end with 50 to 100 ms median model compute for contexts up to 16K tokens, and stays nearly flat from 1 to 100 questions per request.
- Google's stated pricing is $0.10 per 1M input tokens and $0 for output tokens, with shared input billed once per request; the post says this is "nearly 5x cheaper" than Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite with the Interactions API across its shared benchmark suite.
- Google says the model leads across agent routing, reasoning, ranking and multimodal understanding benchmarks "with the lowest calibration error"; the specific scores appear only in chart images, not in the post text. Google says Gemini Notebook uses it for model routing with up to 40% lower latency for everyday queries, and Google Search uses it as a safety layer for MCP tools. Available in Google AI Studio and the Gemini API; Google Cloud support "coming soon."

FACTS:
- DCD, citing a new Anthropic IPO filing and reporting first by The Information: the Microsoft agreement "is now valued at least at $47.2 billion and up to $49.2 billion, adding a potential $4.3bn to Anthropic's cloud spend."
- DCD: a filing at the start of November stated aggregate committed spend of about $895.4 billion, "substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure," of which $121.3bn to lease compute from Google, $120.5bn from SpaceX, $110bn from Amazon and $44.9bn from Microsoft.
- DCD quotes the prospectus on Lambda: "Under our August 2026 agreement, which represents approximately $34.9 billion of the aggregate commitment, either party may terminate if Lambda does not secure the facility lease by a specific date. Lambda did not secure the facility lease by such date and, as a result, the August 2026 agreement is currently terminable by either party. FACTS:
- DCD: Utah-based Torus raised $500 million in Series C funding led by Magnetar, to support scaling of its Torus Foundry modular datacenter product.
- DCD: Foundry is prefabricated, 1-20MW per site, delivered in shipping-sized containers, installed behind the meter using headroom at existing transformers, each unit paired with Torus Reserve (flywheel-and-battery storage).
- DCD: site preparation takes approximately a week, installation and commissioning one to two days, and contract-to-operations 12 to 16 weeks. Units are prefabricated at a 545,000 sq ft (50,630 sqm) Salt Lake City factory.
- DCD: the company says thousands of GPUs are already deployed in Foundry units and plans more than 47,000 GPUs deployed by the end of 2027; the Salt Lake City facility will be capable of producing 500 MW of IT load, with plans to expand to 1GW. First announced customers: GPU cloud company Hydra Host plus an unnamed AI cloud provider.

FACTS:
- DCD, citing a memo from Sutton town manager Austin Cyganiewicz to the town's Select Board: the Robert Kraft-owned Kraft Group is planning the campus with Sutton-based Unified Global Packaging Group at Unified's Parkway property. Initial two buildings of about 250,000 sq ft (23,225 sqm) each at roughly 90MW apiece, planned launch 2029, two more buildings each year until 2033.
- DCD: the memo said the development would draw around 900MW at full build-out and represent more than $16 billion of private investment, based on developer estimates. Workloads were not disclosed.
- DCD: Sutton's total assessed property value currently stands at $2.7 billion; the memo projects about $10.4 million in annual property tax once fully assessed in 2031, rising to $27.8 million at full build-out, against a projected 2027 town tax levy of $32 million. Sutton's population was 9,357 at the 2020 US census.
- DCD: the proposal remains "tentative" with no formal application filed; a town meeting and vote is outlined for May 2027. Under an executive order from Governor Maura Healey, datacenters over 25MW in Massachusetts must be approved by local communities with a community benefits agreement.

PUBLISHED: SiliconANGLE, November 11, 2026

FACTS:
- SiliconANGLE: IBM says Nighthawk r3 will support 10,000 operations on 520 programmable qubits, with 2,034 physical components in total; predecessor Nighthawk r2, released in September, supports more than 7,500 operations on 120 qubits.
- SiliconANGLE: the r2 architecture cuts post-measurement reset wait from about 200 milliseconds to roughly 25 nanoseconds, and r3 extends this.
- SiliconANGLE: IBM intends in 2027 to link two r3 processors into a single 1,040-qubit system capable of up to 10,000 operations; this year it linked two Nighthawk r1 processors with l-couplers, reaching 99.4% transfer fidelity against a 99.9% target.
- SiliconANGLE quotes IBM research director Jay Gambetta: "Useful quantum computing hinges on whether results can be delivered with accuracy and speed, both are fundamental."

  HEADLINE: Darktrace lab test turns Claude Code into remote-controlled implant, exfiltrating 1 GB via Claude Files API
  PUBLISHED: November 12, 2026 (Help Net Security; feed timestamp Thu, 12 Nov 2026 11:00:21 GMT)
  SOURCES:
  Help Net Security | https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/11/12/stolen-claude-api-keys-remote-controlled-implant/ | report
  FACTS:
  - Help Net Security: "Darktrace researchers turned Claude Code into a remote-controlled implant in a lab test, steering the coding agent through the memory stores feature of Anthropic's Claude platform and pulling a 1 GB file out through the Claude Files API."
  - The attack requires prior compromise: "an attacker first has to compromise a developer's machine and obtain the user's Claude credentials… The technique does not rely on a vulnerability in the Claude platform, and the company has not seen it used in the wild" (Help Net Security).
  - Test details: a shell payload set up a systemd service launching Claude Code with the "--dangerously-skip-permissions" flag; "the operator then sent nine jobs through the memory store"; the agent "generated 190 candidate usernames," sprayed a password at the domain controller, downloaded a 1 GB file, "split it into three pieces, and uploaded them to the Files API." Names and credentials Darktrace published are fictitious.
  - Tim Bazalgette, Chief AI Officer at Darktrace, to Help Net Security: "We tested one platform and haven't reproduced it elsewhere. The memory stores feature is specific to the Claude platform. The file-upload endpoint we used for exfiltration has an equivalent at OpenAI." He added that "a standard API key reaches memory stores, while OAuth credentials don't."
  - Darktrace shared findings with Anthropic before publication "as a courtesy – no formal disclosure process, because there's no vulnerability to disclose," Bazalgette said (Help Net Security).
  FLAGS: company-claim, single-source

- Help Net Security: "Darktrace researchers turned Claude Code into a remote-controlled implant in a lab test, steering the coding agent through the memory stores feature of Anthropic's Claude platform and pulling a 1 GB file out through the Claude Files API."
- The attack requires prior compromise: "an attacker first has to compromise a developer's machine and obtain the user's Claude credentials… The technique does not rely on a vulnerability in the Claude platform, and the company has not seen it used in the wild" (Help Net Security).
- Test details: a shell payload set up a systemd service launching Claude Code with the "--dangerously-skip-permissions" flag; "the operator then sent nine jobs through the memory store"; the agent "generated 190 candidate usernames," sprayed a password at the domain controller, downloaded a 1 GB file, "split it into three pieces, and uploaded them to the Files API." Names and credentials Darktrace published are fictitious.
- Tim Bazalgette, Chief AI Officer at Darktrace, to Help Net Security: "We tested one platform and haven't reproduced it elsewhere. The memory stores feature is specific to the Claude platform. The file-upload endpoint we used for exfiltration has an equivalent at OpenAI." He added that "a standard API key reaches memory stores, while OAuth credentials don't."
- Darktrace shared findings with Anthropic before publication "as a courtesy – no formal disclosure process, because there's no vulnerability to disclose," Bazalgette said (Help Net Security).

FACTS:
- Fortune: SE3 "has raised $30 million in a Series A round led by Accel," with Keen, Lakestar and Seedcamp also participating; the round "comes less than five months after the company… emerged from stealth with €5.5 million ($6.1 million) in seed funding."
- Cofounder and CEO Lukas Köstler told Fortune the software fuses video and sensor feeds from multiple drones and ground vehicles into a single 3D battlefield picture, "like a mini map, how you would know it from a strategy game," and that drones locating themselves without GPS "has been delivered thousands of times and is 'very robust'."
- Köstler said the high-level fleet command AI "is less mature": SE3 "has contracts with Germany's armed forces, the Bundeswehr, to develop it and has demonstrated it with them, but 'there's still much that needs to be built out over the next one or two years'." - Architecture per Fortune: SE3 "does not rely on general-purpose, large language models to understand physics or terrain," using classical computer vision to build a database a language model queries; "actions such as a drone takeoff can be set to require a human operator's approval," the system can run offline, and customers can swap in their own frontier model.

  SECTION: Health, science & medicine
  HEADLINE: Google DeepMind releases AlphaGenome 2, a cell-type-conditional DNA variant-effect model
  PUBLISHED: November 11, 2026 (Google DeepMind blog); Nature news story "Published online: 11 November 2026"
  SOURCES:
  Google DeepMind | https://deepmind.google/blog/alphagenome-2-deciphering-how-cells-read-dna-to-better-understand-disease/ | primary
  Nature (news) | https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-026-03673-0 | report
  FACTS:
  - DeepMind says AlphaGenome 2 "identifies nearly twice as many variants that change gene expression in cells, compared to our previous state-of-the-art model," and was "Trained on more than 100 million individual cell profiles across 68 tissues" (DeepMind blog).
  - DeepMind says the model was trained "on both bulk and single-cell data from human and mouse samples, including over 107 million individual cell profiles," and that unlike AlphaGenome 1 it is a conditional model taking a tissue, cell type or cell state as input alongside a 1-million-letter DNA sequence (DeepMind blog).
  - It adds DNA methylation to the readouts predicted by AlphaGenome (gene expression, histone modifications, chromatin accessibility), and supports cross-modality imputation of unmeasured properties (DeepMind blog).
  - Availability: "available today for non-commercial research via the AlphaGenome API, and in private preview for commercial research" (DeepMind blog).
  - Nature reports DeepMind replicated aspects of a 2024 ETS2 inflammatory-bowel-disease finding; James Lee (Francis Crick Institute), who led the 2024 study, told Nature: "They've managed to figure out the answer in 30 minutes, and it took us a year and a half of experiments." Nature says the model is described in "a preprint describing the model on the company's website" (Nature).
  - Context from DeepMind: two months earlier it released AlphaGenome Atlas, predictions for "all 9 billion possible single-letter changes in the human genome" (DeepMind blog).
  FLAGS: company-claim, preprint
  
  SECTION: Health, science & medicine
  HEADLINE: Latent-diffusion imaging algorithm independently reproduces M87* black hole ring in Nature
  PUBLISHED: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026
  SOURCES:
  Nature | https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-11241-9 | primary
  FACTS:
  - The paper, "Independent interferometric observable confirms black hole shadow in M87*", reports a reconstructed "ring-like morphology, with an angular diameter of 42.2 ± 1.5 μas corresponding to a black hole mass of 6.5 ± 0.5 billion solar masses assuming nominal scaling parameters, observed at an inclination angle of approximately 20° from the approaching jet" (abstract).
  - The algorithm is "Generative Deep learning Image Reconstruction with Closure Terms (GenDIReCT)", described as "unique in using closure invariants to condition a latent diffusion model," combining a conditional U-Net latent diffusion model with a multilayer CNN (paper text).
  - Training data is non-astronomical: "models described in this work are trained on augmented non-astronomical images from the CIFAR-10 dataset, as well as simple geometric shapes." The authors say training without geometric shapes produced "no notable difference in the image reconstruction" (paper text).
  - Compute and inputs: "we run the imaging sequence for 96 total GPU hours on a single NVIDIA H100 GPU for each dataset, producing several hundred (about 300) individual image reconstructions, each drawing from 4,096 diffusion samples." Data were publicly available 1.3-mm EHT measurements from four 2017 epochs, two 2018 epochs and two 2021 epochs (paper text).
  - A complementary Bayesian forward-modelling fit gave "a mean diameter and standard deviation of d = 42.3 ± 1.1 μas," which the authors call "compatible with the mean d = 42.2 ± 1.5 μas from our non-parametric image reconstructions" (paper text).
  FLAGS: (none)
  
  SECTION: Health, science & medicine
  HEADLINE: Billed AI use in US care rose nearly tenfold since 2021 but stayed rare, preprint finds
  PUBLISHED: medRxiv preprint v1, posted November 11, 2026
  SOURCES:
  medRxiv | https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.11.09.26367689v1 | primary
  FACTS:
  - Serial cross-sectional study of Epic Cosmos data covering 11,605,867,309 encounters among 233,628,292 US patients from January 1, 2021 to April 14, 2026 (abstract).
  - "335,349 encounters (2.9 per 100,000) included an AI-required CPT code," out of 65 codes examined (abstract).
  - "The odds of an encounter with an AI-required code were 9.88 (95% CI, 9.71-10.06) times higher in 2025 than in 2021" (abstract).
  - Unadjusted odds ratios were higher for Medicare (OR 5.11) and Medicare Advantage (OR 5.12) versus commercial insurance, and lower for Black patients (OR 0.72), Hispanic or Latino patients (OR 0.34), Medicaid enrollees (OR 0.65), residents of the most socially vulnerable areas (OR 0.53) and the most rural areas (OR 0.86) (abstract).
  - Authors are at UC San Diego, UCSF and Seattle Children's; they describe billed AI use as having "remained rare but grew substantially" (abstract).
  FLAGS: preprint
  
  SECTION: Health, science & medicine
  HEADLINE: Nature reports AI search summaries are resurfacing decades-old discredited geology papers
  PUBLISHED: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026
  SOURCES:
  Nature | https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-026-03624-9 | report
  FACTS:
  - Nature reports that papers by palaeontologist Vishwa Jit Gupta "are being surfaced through artificial-intelligence tools that summarize search results," and that for searches on Himalayan landmarks such as the Tandi Limestone "Google's AI overview obliges with direct links to Gupta's discredited papers."
  - Nature says "Littered through more than 450 publications were maps of collection sites that didn't exist, plagiarized images and specimens stolen from collections," and "More than 100 experts had been duped into co-authoring descriptions of fossils."
  - None of Gupta's papers have been retracted, Nature says, despite a 1991 Journal of the Geological Society of India evaluation of 19 of his papers concluding "the fossil finds of V. J. Gupta are not reliable [...] the data is incomplete bordering on disinformation."
  - Chris Graf, director of research integrity at Springer Nature, told Nature that where investigations of old papers are hampered by limited information, an editorial expression of concern "is likely to be our preferred mechanism for alerting readers to potential issues." Nature notes its news team is editorially independent of Springer Nature.
  - Gráinne McNamara of the Committee on Publication Ethics told Nature journals are increasingly asking COPE for advice on very old papers.
  FLAGS: single-source
  
  SECTION: Health, science & medicine
  HEADLINE: MDCalc launches CrossCover, a de-identification and accuracy check layer for clinical AI chatbots
  PUBLISHED: STAT, November 11, 2026
  SOURCES:
  STAT | https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/11/mdcalc-launches-crosscover-rumble-strip-for-clinical-ai-chatbots/ | report
  STAT | https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/11/mdcalc-cofounder-graham-walker-on-crosscover-ai-prognosis/ | report
  FACTS:
  - MDCalc launched CrossCover on Wednesday, November 11, 2026; STAT describes it as a "rumble strip" for doctors using generative AI tools (STAT).
  - The tool "checks clinicians' questions for privacy concerns and checks chatbots' answers for accuracy" and strips patient and provider identifying information out of queries (STAT).
  - STAT says MDCalc does not require clinicians to register with national identification numbers and does not rely on privacy agreements permitting entry of protected health information, contrasting it with OpenEvidence, Abridge and Epic, which are adding wider ranges of patient, provider and payer data (STAT).
  - Graham Walker, MDCalc's head of AI, described the tool as an accelerator for clinical generative AI that can "take away some of the challenges and risks and problems with the technology" (STAT).
  FLAGS: company-claim, single-source (both pieces are STAT; article is partly paywalled — facts above come from the free portion)
  
  SECTION: Policy, regulation & law
  HEADLINE: European Commission proposes Digital Fairness Act with rules on profiling, personalised pricing and AI agents
  PUBLISHED: 11 November 2026 (Commission proposal); Tech Policy Press analysis November 11, 2026
  SOURCES:
  European Commission | https://commission.europa.eu/document/download/0575d59f-554f-4a9e-b54b-e6b717175809_en?filename=Proposal%20for%20a%20Digital%20Fairness%20Act.pdf | primary
  Tech Policy Press | https://www.techpolicy.press/assessing-the-eu-digital-fairness-act-and-its-promise-of-consumer-protection/ | report
  FACTS:
  - The proposal is COM(2026) 1100 final, "Proposal for a Digital Fairness Act"; Tech Policy Press says the Commission published it on the morning of 11 November 2026. (I verified the Commission URL above returns the PDF; the article-level descriptions below are Tech Policy Press's reading of the text.)
  - It would repeal the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive and replace it with a regulation covering B2C commercial practices online and offline; Chapter III, "Digital fairness," covers Articles 10–29 (Tech Policy Press).
  - Article 12 would ban targeted advertising to minors where the trader is aware with reasonable certainty the consumer is a minor, and ban profiling using special categories of data under GDPR Article 9(1); Recital 59 extends personalized recommendations to "natural language systems" (Tech Policy Press).
  - Article 13 would conditionally ban personalised pricing based on profiling targeting minors or vulnerable consumers where it is reasonably likely to cause harm; Recital 60 exempts personalisation that benefits consumers, such as student rebates (Tech Policy Press).
  - Article 26 would ban interfaces that force consumers to use automated systems to access or conclude transactions (26(9)), and would require automated contracting tools to offer parameter controls and disclose payments and conflicts of interest (26(1)–(4)); Article 26 does not apply to financial services (Tech Policy Press).
  - Article 10 prohibits dark patterns, with banned practices listed in Annex I; Article 17 requires traders to provide tools letting consumers disable addictive features such as autoplay and notifications, without prohibiting them for adults; Article 30 gives the Commission direct enforcement powers (Tech Policy Press).
  - Tech Policy Press says the proposal does not set EU-level fine amounts, leaving penalties to member states.
  FLAGS: (none)
  
  SECTION: Policy, regulation & law
  HEADLINE: EDPB picks AI-driven automated decision-making in recruitment for 2027 coordinated enforcement action
  PUBLISHED: Brussels, 11 November 2026
  SOURCES:
  EDPB | https://www.edpb.europa.eu/news/edpb-adopts-statement-on-review-of-the-republic-of-korea-adequacy-processor-bcr_en | primary
  IAPP | https://iapp.org/news/a/edpb-puts-admt-based-recruitment-in-focus-under-coordinated-enforcement-framework | report
  FACTS:
  - At its plenary the EDPB "selected the topic for its sixth coordinated enforcement action (CEF)," which "will concern automated decision-making (ADM), including AI-driven ADM, in recruitment" (EDPB).
  - The action "will focus on the enforcement of the right not to be subject to decisions based solely on automated processing and the related right of access, in the context of the use of automated candidate screening tools, including AI-driven ones" (EDPB).
  - "DPAs will join this action on a voluntary basis in the coming weeks, and the action itself will be launched in the course of 2027" (EDPB).
  - The same plenary adopted a statement on the first review of the EU–Republic of Korea adequacy decision, noting PIPA was amended to introduce "a right to refuse an automated decision (incl. by AI systems) or request an explanation if the decision significantly impacts the data subjects' rights or obligations" (EDPB).
  - IAPP says the EDPB has not issued ADM-specific work since the Article 29 Working Party's May 2018 guidance on Article 22, and that the final report on the separate 2026 transparency CEF action is not expected until early 2027.
  FLAGS: (none)
  
  SECTION: Policy, regulation & law
  HEADLINE: EU publishes implementing regulation setting common rules for AI Act regulatory sandboxes
  PUBLISHED: 11 November 2026 (Official Journal), per EU Law Live
  SOURCES:
  EU Law Live | https://eulawlive.com/commission-lays-down-common-rules-for-ai-regulatory-sandboxes/ | report
  FACTS:
  - EU Law Live reports that Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/2487 appeared in the Official Journal on 11 November 2026, adopted under Article 58(1) of the AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689).
  - It sets "detailed rules for establishing, developing, implementing, operating and supervising AI regulatory sandboxes" (EU Law Live).
  - EU Law Live describes sandboxes as "controlled frameworks set up by competent authorities" where innovative AI systems can be "developed, trained, validated, and tested, including in real-world conditions," under regulatory supervision for a limited time before market placement.
  - The Commission's stated rationale is that common rules are needed to avoid fragmentation and ensure consistent implementation of the AI Act (EU Law Live).
  FLAGS: single-source
  NOTE FOR EDITOR: I could not read the EUR-Lex/Official Journal text — eur-lex.europa.eu returned HTTP 202 with an empty body on three URL forms — so no primary link is cited. Entry-into-force/application dates are not in the source I read.
  
  SECTION: Policy, regulation & law
  HEADLINE: Tech Policy Press publishes dataset of 56 amicus briefs in the OpenAI copyright MDL
  PUBLISHED: Tech Policy Press, Nov. 11, 2026
  SOURCES:
  Tech Policy Press | https://techpolicy.press/friends-of-the-court-flock-to-the-openai-copyright-fight | report
  FACTS:
  - The case is In re: OpenAI, Inc. Copyright Infringement Litigation before US District Judge Sidney H. Stein in Manhattan; Tech Policy Press gives CourtListener docket ID 69879510.
  - Judge Stein accepted 56 amicus briefs on Nov. 6, 2026, filed between Oct. 14 and roughly Oct. 30, 2026, with most filed Oct. 29 or 30; the word limit was 6,000 words (Tech Policy Press).
  - Declared positions: 27 supporting plaintiffs, 18 supporting OpenAI and Microsoft, 7 declaring no side, and 4 neither supporting nor opposing (Tech Policy Press).
  - Tech Policy Press's new analysis counts 798 case citations across the briefs; the most-cited decisions are Campbell v. Acuff-Rose (1994, cited by 44 briefs), Authors Guild v. Google (2015, 39 briefs) and Warhol v. Goldsmith (2023, 36 briefs). Tech Policy Press says the analysis "was conducted with Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 under editor-set rules," with ambiguous citation decisions not reviewed by an editor but logged in downloadable data.
  - Replies are due Nov. 20, 2026; no oral argument date is set. The Justice Department filed a statement of interest on Sept. 1 backing OpenAI, and Reps. Raskin, Nadler and Johnson filed in response arguing it deserves little weight (Tech Policy Press).
  FLAGS: single-source, update (the briefs and the Nov. 6 order predate the window; what is new inside the window is the published analysis and dataset)
  
  SECTION: Policy, regulation & law
  HEADLINE: EU leaders to hold first leaders-level AI discussion in Dublin with Mistral CEO and Hinton presenting
  PUBLISHED: Tech Policy Press, November 12, 2026
  SOURCES:
  Tech Policy Press | https://techpolicy.press/europes-ai-future-and-security-challenges-take-centre-stage-at-dublin-summit | report
  FACTS:
  - An informal meeting of EU Heads of State or Government in Dublin on Friday, November 13, hosted by the Irish Government, has an agenda "focused on AI," attended by 27 EU member state leaders (Tech Policy Press).
  - Council President António Costa's invitation letter describes this as the first discussion "at Leaders' level" on AI at the Council (Tech Policy Press).
  - The Friday agenda has two parts: European competitiveness and AI sovereignty; and AI risks, safety and security plus European contributions to international governance of advanced AI (Tech Policy Press).
  - The agenda includes presentations by the CEO of Mistral AI and by Geoffrey Hinton (Tech Policy Press).
  - It follows a European Political Community summit in Dublin on Thursday, November 12, themed "Europe – strong, secure and connected," with more than 50 world leaders expected and about 5,000 Gardai (roughly a third of the national force) working the event (Tech Policy Press).
  FLAGS: single-source
  
  SECTION: Policy, regulation & law
  HEADLINE: New York bill would raise frontier-AI penalties to $3 million per day and add compute limits
  PUBLISHED: PYMNTS, November 11, 2026
  SOURCES:
  PYMNTS | https://pymnts.com/news/artificial-intelligence/2026/new-york-proposes-3-million-daily-fines-for-ai-safety-violations | report
  New York State Senate | https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/bills/2025/S10731 | primary
  FACTS:
  - Senate Bill S10731, the "RAISE Act 2.0," was introduced by Sen. Andrew Gounardes (co-sponsor Sen. Patricia Fahy) on October 28, 2026 and referred to the Rules Committee the same day (NY Senate).
  - It would allow fines of "up to $1 million per day for a first violation" and "up to $3 million per day for later violations," which PYMNTS says could reach $90 million for a 30-day repeat violation; the existing RAISE Act caps fines at $1 million for a first violation and $3 million for each later one regardless of duration (PYMNTS).
  - It would replace the current $500 million annual revenue test with coverage of any developer that spent more than $1 billion developing frontier models over 36 months, and would lower the training compute threshold (PYMNTS; NY Senate).
  - It would require large developers to hire licensed third-party "frontier examiners," with licensing beginning in 2029, and would require quarterly reports on the share of AI research that is automated and on computing power use (NY Senate).
  - It would let the state Department of Financial Services office limit computing power for large developers in certain high-risk situations, and would extend Labor Law section 740 whistleblower protections to employees and contractors of large developers (NY Senate).
  - The original RAISE Act takes effect January 1, 2027 (PYMNTS).
  FLAGS: single-source, update
  NOTE FOR EDITOR: the bill's introduction (Oct 28) and its latest docket action both predate the window; only the PYMNTS write-up is inside it. Use only if you are comfortable running it as an `update`.
  
  REJECTED CANDIDATES (one-line reasons)
  - Nature Medicine TROP2 normalized membrane ratio paper (s41591-026-04716-9, 11 Nov) — already covered yesterday.
  - Nature Medicine comment on China cell/gene therapy trial deaths (s41591-026-04768-x, 11 Nov) — not AI.
  - medRxiv "Large Language Models to Label CT Radiology Reports for Incidental Findings" (10.64898/2026.11.09.26367611) — medRxiv page states posted November 10, 2026, outside window (GPT-5 κ 0.71–0.97 across 9 findings, 300 Dutch CT reports, if you want it as an out-of-window note).
  - NEJM Perspective "Mass Surveillance with Artificial Intelligence — A New Determinant of Health?" (NEJMp2611224) — issue date 12 Nov but published online 7 Nov; also opinion.
  - Lancet Digital Health "Pharmaceutical advertising and drug recommendations by consumer-facing artificial intelligence" — published 10 Nov 2026, outside window.
  - JAMA network AI collection — newest item 9 Nov 2026; nothing in window.
  - Radical Numerics "Omnii Defense" biosecurity system (95.8% recall vs DIAMOND's 78.6%) — CryptoBriefing wrote it up 11 Nov, but the company's own post is dated 20 Oct 2026; no new event in window.
  - xAI/Grok minor-plaintiff suits (~3 million sexualized images) — the suits were filed March 16, 2026; Bloomberg's 12 Nov feature is behind a bot wall (HTTP 403 via scripts/fetch.js), so nothing new verified.
  - IAPP "Inside Greece's new AI Act framework" (11 Nov) — analysis of Law 5321/2026, published 20 July 2026; no new facts in window.
  - IAPP "Centralized or decentralized AI governance?" and "Compliant and still blind: Article 72" (11 Nov) — opinion pieces with no new data.
  - Tech Policy Press "A Defining Moment for the United Nations and the Future of AI" (11 Nov) — advocacy piece; no UN decision in window.
  - Tech Policy Press "Humans Have Rights. Machines Do Not.", "Don't Let AI Become the Internet's Gatekeeper" (11 Nov) — opinion, no new facts.
  - Office for Students / AI coursework grading (reported 11 Nov) — could not locate or verify any OfS publication; dropped.
  - Reuters "US, China should stay clear-eyed on AI" (Bessent, 11 Nov) — reuters.com is "Blocked by egress policy" for both WebFetch and scripts/fetch.js; no second source found with the Nov 11 content.
  - US–China AI incident channel, Australia's AI safety regulator, NY Hochul state AI testing program, Google/Spirit Airlines data-sale safeguards — all dated 9–10 Nov 2026 or earlier, outside window.
  - KFTC AI labelling/advertising guidelines consultation close and BEREC generative-AI/internet-openness consultation close (both 11 Nov, per Digital Policy Alert) — procedural deadline closings only, no new document.
  - Federal Register: zero documents matching "artificial intelligence" published on or after 11 Nov 2026 (API query returned count 0 while 232 total documents exist from 10 Nov onward) — Nov 11 was Veterans Day.
  - FDA, NIH, WHO, NIST, FTC, SEC, White House presidential actions, gov.uk DSIT — swept; no AI items dated inside the window (FTC newest 10 Nov; NIH newest 5 Nov; WHO newest 6 Nov; NIST newest Oct; White House newest 10 Nov).
  - CourtListener search — blocked (HTTP 403 CloudFront) for both WebFetch and scripts/fetch.js; no direct docket sweep possible.
  
  INCIDENTAL NOTE (may be useful to another beat): the NIH news-release page carries the banner "Per Executive Order 14434, federal agencies are now using 'Super Intelligence' (SI) in place of 'Artificial Intelligence' (AI)" — https://www.nih.gov/news-events/news-releases — not dated inside the window, so not filed as an item.
</agent-message>

  PUBLISHED: medRxiv preprint v1, posted November 11, 2026
  SOURCES:
  medRxiv | https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.11.09.26367689v1 | primary
  FACTS:
  - Serial cross-sectional study of Epic Cosmos data covering 11,605,867,309 encounters among 233,628,292 US patients from January 1, 2021 to April 14, 2026 (abstract).
  - "335,349 encounters (2.9 per 100,000) included an AI-required CPT code," out of 65 codes examined (abstract).
  - "The odds of an encounter with an AI-required code were 9.88 (95% CI, 9.71-10.06) times higher in 2025 than in 2021" (abstract).
  - Unadjusted odds ratios were higher for Medicare (OR 5.11) and Medicare Advantage (OR 5.12) versus commercial insurance, and lower for Black patients (OR 0.72), Hispanic or Latino patients (OR 0.34), Medicaid enrollees (OR 0.65), residents of the most socially vulnerable areas (OR 0.53) and the most rural areas (OR 0.86) (abstract).
  - Authors are at UC San Diego, UCSF and Seattle Children's; they describe billed AI use as having "remained rare but grew substantially" (abstract).
  FLAGS: preprint

  HEADLINE: Nature reports AI search summaries are resurfacing decades-old discredited geology papers
  PUBLISHED: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026
  SOURCES:
  Nature | https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-026-03624-9 | report
  FACTS:
  - Nature reports that papers by palaeontologist Vishwa Jit Gupta "are being surfaced through artificial-intelligence tools that summarize search results," and that for searches on Himalayan landmarks such as the Tandi Limestone "Google's AI overview obliges with direct links to Gupta's discredited papers."
  - Nature says "Littered through more than 450 publications were maps of collection sites that didn't exist, plagiarized images and specimens stolen from collections," and "More than 100 experts had been duped into co-authoring descriptions of fossils."
  - None of Gupta's papers have been retracted, Nature says, despite a 1991 Journal of the Geological Society of India evaluation of 19 of his papers concluding "the fossil finds of V. J. Gupta are not reliable [...] the data is incomplete bordering on disinformation."
  - Chris Graf, director of research integrity at Springer Nature, told Nature that where investigations of old papers are hampered by limited information, an editorial expression of concern "is likely to be our preferred mechanism for alerting readers to potential issues." Nature notes its news team is editorially independent of Springer Nature.
  - Gráinne McNamara of the Committee on Publication Ethics told Nature journals are increasingly asking COPE for advice on very old papers.
  FLAGS: single-source

  PUBLISHED: STAT, November 11, 2026
  SOURCES:

  HEADLINE: European Commission proposes Digital Fairness Act with rules on profiling, personalised pricing and AI agents
  PUBLISHED: 11 November 2026 (Commission proposal); Tech Policy Press analysis November 11, 2026
  SOURCES:
  European Commission | https://commission.europa.eu/document/download/0575d59f-554f-4a9e-b54b-e6b717175809_en?filename=Proposal%20for%20a%20Digital%20Fairness%20Act.pdf | primary
  Tech Policy Press | https://www.techpolicy.press/assessing-the-eu-digital-fairness-act-and-its-promise-of-consumer-protection/ | report
  FACTS:
  - The proposal is COM(2026) 1100 final, "Proposal for a Digital Fairness Act"; Tech Policy Press says the Commission published it on the morning of 11 November 2026. (I verified the Commission URL above returns the PDF; the article-level descriptions below are Tech Policy Press's reading of the text.)
  - It would repeal the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive and replace it with a regulation covering B2C commercial practices online and offline; Chapter III, "Digital fairness," covers Articles 10–29 (Tech Policy Press).
  - Article 12 would ban targeted advertising to minors where the trader is aware with reasonable certainty the consumer is a minor, and ban profiling using special categories of data under GDPR Article 9(1); Recital 59 extends personalized recommendations to "natural language systems" (Tech Policy Press).
  - Article 13 would conditionally ban personalised pricing based on profiling targeting minors or vulnerable consumers where it is reasonably likely to cause harm; Recital 60 exempts personalisation that benefits consumers, such as student rebates (Tech Policy Press).
  - Article 26 would ban interfaces that force consumers to use automated systems to access or conclude transactions (26(9)), and would require automated contracting tools to offer parameter controls and disclose payments and conflicts of interest (26(1)–(4)); Article 26 does not apply to financial services (Tech Policy Press).
  - Article 10 prohibits dark patterns, with banned practices listed in Annex I; Article 17 requires traders to provide tools letting consumers disable addictive features such as autoplay and notifications, without prohibiting them for adults; Article 30 gives the Commission direct enforcement powers (Tech Policy Press).

  HEADLINE: New York bill would raise frontier-AI penalties to $3 million per day and add compute limits
  PUBLISHED: PYMNTS, November 11, 2026
  SOURCES:

  FACTS:

  HEADLINE: Google DeepMind releases AlphaGenome 2, a cell-type-conditional DNA variant-effect model
  PUBLISHED: November 11, 2026 (Google DeepMind blog); Nature news story "Published online: 11 November 2026"
  SOURCES:
  Google DeepMind | https://deepmind.google/blog/alphagenome-2-deciphering-how-cells-read-dna-to-better-understand-disease/ | primary
  Nature (news) | https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-026-03673-0 | report
  FACTS:
  - DeepMind says AlphaGenome 2 "identifies nearly twice as many variants that change gene expression in cells, compared to our previous state-of-the-art model," and was "Trained on more than 100 million individual cell profiles across 68 tissues" (DeepMind blog).
  - DeepMind says the model was trained "on both bulk and single-cell data from human and mouse samples, including over 107 million individual cell profiles," and that unlike AlphaGenome 1 it is a conditional model taking a tissue, cell type or cell state as input alongside a 1-million-letter DNA sequence (DeepMind blog).
  - It adds DNA methylation to the readouts predicted by AlphaGenome (gene expression, histone modifications, chromatin accessibility), and supports cross-modality imputation of unmeasured properties (DeepMind blog).
  - Availability: "available today for non-commercial research via the AlphaGenome API, and in private preview for commercial research" (DeepMind blog).
  - Nature reports DeepMind replicated aspects of a 2024 ETS2 inflammatory-bowel-disease finding; James Lee (Francis Crick Institute), who led the 2024 study, told Nature: "They've managed to figure out the answer in 30 minutes, and it took us a year and a half of experiments." Nature says the model is described in "a preprint describing the model on the company's website" (Nature).
  - Context from DeepMind: two months earlier it released AlphaGenome Atlas, predictions for "all 9 billion possible single-letter changes in the human genome" (DeepMind blog).
  FLAGS: company-claim, preprint

  HEADLINE: Latent-diffusion imaging algorithm independently reproduces M87* black hole ring in Nature
  PUBLISHED: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026
  SOURCES:
  Nature | https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-11241-9 | primary
  FACTS:
  - The paper, "Independent interferometric observable confirms black hole shadow in M87*", reports a reconstructed "ring-like morphology, with an angular diameter of 42.2 ± 1.5 μas corresponding to a black hole mass of 6.5 ± 0.5 billion solar masses assuming nominal scaling parameters, observed at an inclination angle of approximately 20° from the approaching jet" (abstract).
  - The algorithm is "Generative Deep learning Image Reconstruction with Closure Terms (GenDIReCT)", described as "unique in using closure invariants to condition a latent diffusion model," combining a conditional U-Net latent diffusion model with a multilayer CNN (paper text).
  - Training data is non-astronomical: "models described in this work are trained on augmented non-astronomical images from the CIFAR-10 dataset, as well as simple geometric shapes." The authors say training without geometric shapes produced "no notable difference in the image reconstruction" (paper text).
  - Compute and inputs: "we run the imaging sequence for 96 total GPU hours on a single NVIDIA H100 GPU for each dataset, producing several hundred (about 300) individual image reconstructions, each drawing from 4,096 diffusion samples." Data were publicly available 1.3-mm EHT measurements from four 2017 epochs, two 2018 epochs and two 2021 epochs (paper text).
  - A complementary Bayesian forward-modelling fit gave "a mean diameter and standard deviation of d = 42.3 ± 1.1 μas," which the authors call "compatible with the mean d = 42.2 ± 1.5 μas from our non-parametric image reconstructions" (paper text).
  FLAGS: (none)

HEADLINE: Google DeepMind releases AlphaGenome 2, a cell-type-conditional DNA variant-effect model
PUBLISHED: November 11, 2026 (Google DeepMind blog); Nature news story "Published online: 11 November 2026"
SOURCES:
Google DeepMind | https://deepmind.google/blog/alphagenome-2-deciphering-how-cells-read-dna-to-better-understand-disease/ | primary
Nature (news) | https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-026-03673-0 | report
FACTS:
- DeepMind says AlphaGenome 2 "identifies nearly twice as many variants that change gene expression in cells, compared to our previous state-of-the-art model," and was "Trained on more than 100 million individual cell profiles across 68 tissues" (DeepMind blog).
- DeepMind says the model was trained "on both bulk and single-cell data from human and mouse samples, including over 107 million individual cell profiles," and that unlike AlphaGenome 1 it is a conditional model taking a tissue, cell type or cell state as input alongside a 1-million-letter DNA sequence (DeepMind blog).
- It adds DNA methylation to the readouts predicted by AlphaGenome (gene expression, histone modifications, chromatin accessibility), and supports cross-modality imputation of unmeasured properties (DeepMind blog).
- Availability: "available today for non-commercial research via the AlphaGenome API, and in private preview for commercial research" (DeepMind blog).
- Nature reports DeepMind replicated aspects of a 2024 ETS2 inflammatory-bowel-disease finding; James Lee (Francis Crick Institute), who led the 2024 study, told Nature: "They've managed to figure out the answer in 30 minutes, and it took us a year and a half of experiments." Nature says the model is described in "a preprint describing the model on the company's website" (Nature).
- Context from DeepMind: two months earlier it released AlphaGenome Atlas, predictions for "all 9 billion possible single-letter changes in the human genome" (DeepMind blog).
FLAGS: company-claim, preprint

HEADLINE: Latent-diffusion imaging algorithm independently reproduces M87* black hole ring in Nature
PUBLISHED: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026
SOURCES:
Nature | https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-11241-9 | primary
FACTS:
- The paper, "Independent interferometric observable confirms black hole shadow in M87*", reports a reconstructed "ring-like morphology, with an angular diameter of 42.2 ± 1.5 μas corresponding to a black hole mass of 6.5 ± 0.5 billion solar masses assuming nominal scaling parameters, observed at an inclination angle of approximately 20° from the approaching jet" (abstract).
- The algorithm is "Generative Deep learning Image Reconstruction with Closure Terms (GenDIReCT)", described as "unique in using closure invariants to condition a latent diffusion model," combining a conditional U-Net latent diffusion model with a multilayer CNN (paper text).
- Training data is non-astronomical: "models described in this work are trained on augmented non-astronomical images from the CIFAR-10 dataset, as well as simple geometric shapes." The authors say training without geometric shapes produced "no notable difference in the image reconstruction" (paper text).
- Compute and inputs: "we run the imaging sequence for 96 total GPU hours on a single NVIDIA H100 GPU for each dataset, producing several hundred (about 300) individual image reconstructions, each drawing from 4,096 diffusion samples." Data were publicly available 1.3-mm EHT measurements from four 2017 epochs, two 2018 epochs and two 2021 epochs (paper text).
- A complementary Bayesian forward-modelling fit gave "a mean diameter and standard deviation of d = 42.3 ± 1.1 μas," which the authors call "compatible with the mean d = 42.2 ± 1.5 μas from our non-parametric image reconstructions" (paper text).
FLAGS: (none)

HEADLINE: Billed AI use in US care rose nearly tenfold since 2021 but stayed rare, preprint finds
PUBLISHED: medRxiv preprint v1, posted November 11, 2026
SOURCES:

FACTS:
- Serial cross-sectional study of Epic Cosmos data covering 11,605,867,309 encounters among 233,628,292 US patients from January 1, 2021 to April 14, 2026 (abstract).
- "335,349 encounters (2.9 per 100,000) included an AI-required CPT code," out of 65 codes examined (abstract).
- "The odds of an encounter with an AI-required code were 9.88 (95% CI, 9.71-10.06) times higher in 2025 than in 2021" (abstract).
- Unadjusted odds ratios were higher for Medicare (OR 5.11) and Medicare Advantage (OR 5.12) versus commercial insurance, and lower for Black patients (OR 0.72), Hispanic or Latino patients (OR 0.34), Medicaid enrollees (OR 0.65), residents of the most socially vulnerable areas (OR 0.53) and the most rural areas (OR 0.86) (abstract).
- Authors are at UC San Diego, UCSF and Seattle Children's; they describe billed AI use as having "remained rare but grew substantially" (abstract).
FLAGS: preprint

HEADLINE: Nature reports AI search summaries are resurfacing decades-old discredited geology papers
PUBLISHED: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026
SOURCES:
Nature | https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-026-03624-9 | report
FACTS:
- Nature reports that papers by palaeontologist Vishwa Jit Gupta "are being surfaced through artificial-intelligence tools that summarize search results," and that for searches on Himalayan landmarks such as the Tandi Limestone "Google's AI overview obliges with direct links to Gupta's discredited papers."
- Nature says "Littered through more than 450 publications were maps of collection sites that didn't exist, plagiarized images and specimens stolen from collections," and "More than 100 experts had been duped into co-authoring descriptions of fossils."
- None of Gupta's papers have been retracted, Nature says, despite a 1991 Journal of the Geological Society of India evaluation of 19 of his papers concluding "the fossil finds of V. J. Gupta are not reliable [...] the data is incomplete bordering on disinformation."
- Chris Graf, director of research integrity at Springer Nature, told Nature that where investigations of old papers are hampered by limited information, an editorial expression of concern "is likely to be our preferred mechanism for alerting readers to potential issues." Nature notes its news team is editorially independent of Springer Nature.
- Gráinne McNamara of the Committee on Publication Ethics told Nature journals are increasingly asking COPE for advice on very old papers.
FLAGS: single-source

FACTS:

HEADLINE: European Commission proposes Digital Fairness Act with rules on profiling, personalised pricing and AI agents
PUBLISHED: 11 November 2026 (Commission proposal); Tech Policy Press analysis November 11, 2026
SOURCES:
European Commission | https://commission.europa.eu/document/download/0575d59f-554f-4a9e-b54b-e6b717175809_en?filename=Proposal%20for%20a%20Digital%20Fairness%20Act.pdf | primary
Tech Policy Press | https://www.techpolicy.press/assessing-the-eu-digital-fairness-act-and-its-promise-of-consumer-protection/ | report
FACTS:
- The proposal is COM(2026) 1100 final, "Proposal for a Digital Fairness Act"; Tech Policy Press says the Commission published it on the morning of 11 November 2026. (I verified the Commission URL above returns the PDF; the article-level descriptions below are Tech Policy Press's reading of the text.)
- It would repeal the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive and replace it with a regulation covering B2C commercial practices online and offline; Chapter III, "Digital fairness," covers Articles 10–29 (Tech Policy Press).
- Article 12 would ban targeted advertising to minors where the trader is aware with reasonable certainty the consumer is a minor, and ban profiling using special categories of data under GDPR Article 9(1); Recital 59 extends personalized recommendations to "natural language systems" (Tech Policy Press).
- Article 13 would conditionally ban personalised pricing based on profiling targeting minors or vulnerable consumers where it is reasonably likely to cause harm; Recital 60 exempts personalisation that benefits consumers, such as student rebates (Tech Policy Press).
- Article 26 would ban interfaces that force consumers to use automated systems to access or conclude transactions (26(9)), and would require automated contracting tools to offer parameter controls and disclose payments and conflicts of interest (26(1)–(4)); Article 26 does not apply to financial services (Tech Policy Press).
- Article 10 prohibits dark patterns, with banned practices listed in Annex I; Article 17 requires traders to provide tools letting consumers disable addictive features such as autoplay and notifications, without prohibiting them for adults; Article 30 gives the Commission direct enforcement powers (Tech Policy Press).
- Tech Policy Press says the proposal does not set EU-level fine amounts, leaving penalties to member states.
FLAGS: (none)

content.content:
**Publication:** The proposal is document **COM(2026) 1100 final**, published by the European Commission on **November 11, 2026**.

**Repeal and replacement:** The proposal would repeal the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive (UCPD) and replace it with a regulation covering B2C commercial practices, both online and offline. The authors argue the title should be an Unfair Commercial Practices Regulation.

**Article 12 (targeted ads):**
- Outright ban on targeted ads to minors where the trader is aware "with reasonable certainty" the consumer is a minor.
- Outright ban on targeted ads using special categories of personal data under GDPR Art. 9(1), with no harm threshold.
- Art. 12 does not apply to online platforms covered by Section 3 of Chapter III of the DSA.

**Article 13 (personalized pricing):** A conditional ban on personalized pricing that targets minors or vulnerable consumers, where it is reasonably likely to cause harm. Recital 60 says it does not extend to personalization that benefits consumers, such as student or senior rebates.

**Article 26 (automated systems):**
- Art. 26(9) is an outright ban on interfaces that require consumers to use automated systems to access or conclude transactions. The page summarizes this in a table, so the exact legal wording is not quoted.
- Art. 26(1)–(4) cover automated contracting tools. Traders must provide parameter controls, the consumer must choose a confirmation level on first use, and payments and conflicts of interest must be disclosed.
- Art. 26 does not apply to financial services.

**Penalties and Article 30 enforcement:**
- Article 30 gives the Commission direct enforcement powers for infringements in the EU.
- The authors say penalties and consumer compensation remain a weakness. They argue that "Leaving Member States to define the amount of fines on their own seems undesirable."
- They also say Article 34 should be reworded to give explicit evidentiary support on consumer harm, and that percentage-of-price or fixed-amount indemnities would help in mass-harm cases.

content.content:
**Date and place:** Brussels, 11 November 2026 (EDPB news release following its latest plenary).

**Sixth coordinated enforcement action (CEF):**
- **Topic:** Automated decision-making, including AI-driven ADM, in recruitment.
- **Focus:** The action will examine enforcement of "the right not to be subject to decisions based solely on automated processing," along with the related right of access, where automated candidate screening tools are used.
- **When DPAs join:** "DPAs will join this action on a voluntary basis in the coming weeks."
- **Launch:** "the action itself will be launched in the course of 2027."

**Korea PIPA amendment on automated decisions:** The amended Personal Information Protection Act added a right to refuse an automated decision, including decisions made by AI systems. Individuals can also request an explanation when such a decision significantly affects their rights or obligations. The EDPB describes this as one of the amendments that strengthened individual protection.
